passage:
Session note, community centre. Present: Jomon, his wife Anila, and Jomon's mother. The disagreement was about whether the couple should move into the family home. For the first twenty minutes Jomon looked at the floor and said, “Whatever you both think.” His mother and Anila each turned to him, then away, more upset each time he stayed silent. When I asked him to say what he wanted, he took a long breath. “Amma, I hear you. Anila and I will decide about the flat together, and you are welcome every Sunday.” Both women went quiet, then Amma nodded. I suggested the couple talk privately this week before returning.
Nandini, counsellor

qa.q: Who was present at the session besides Jomon?
qa.a: His wife Anila and Jomon's mother were present.

qa.q: Why did Jomon say, “Whatever you both think,” for the first twenty minutes?
qa.a: Jomon seems to be torn and trying to avoid the tension. Staying silent left his mother and Anila each feeling unsupported.

qa.q: What could Jomon and Anila do during the week before returning?
qa.a: They could talk privately about what they want and agree on a shared plan, so Jomon can speak fairly to his mother with Anila's view already heard.

qa.q: How might Jomon's mother have felt when Jomon said, “you are welcome every Sunday”?
qa.a: Jomon's mother may have felt reassured that she is not being pushed away, which fits her going quiet and then nodding.

grounding: A young spouse caught between his mother and his wife avoids the tension by silence, which leaves both unsupported, then takes a calm, fair stand.

passage:
Shalini's diary, Thursday, 11 pm.
Tonight my parents came to dinner and Papa said we should move within a short drive of them. Vishal said he'd like to keep our flat near his office. Then both of them looked at me. I kept passing chapatis. Papa said, “Beta, you decide.” Vishal said nothing and went out to the balcony. I stayed at the table with Mummy and heard myself say, “Let me think.” Now I see my silence helped nobody: it sounded like agreeing with nobody. Tomorrow I'll say to Papa, calmly, that we love them, that we are staying near Vishal's office, and that Sundays are theirs. Then I'll go and sit next to Vishal.

qa.q: Where did Vishal go after saying nothing?
qa.a: Vishal went out to the balcony.

qa.q: What was Shalini feeling when both Papa and Vishal looked at Shalini?
qa.a: Shalini felt torn and cornered by two views and passed chapatis instead of answering, and now sees that the silence helped nobody.

qa.q: What did the writer plan to do about it?
qa.a: Shalini plans to tell Papa calmly that they are staying near Vishal's office and that Sundays are for Papa and Mummy, then to sit beside Vishal.

qa.q: How might Vishal have felt when Shalini said, “Let me think”?
qa.a: Vishal may have felt unsupported and left alone with the disagreement, which fits leaving for the balcony without a word.

grounding: A young spouse torn between their own parents and partner stays silent, sees that it left both unsupported, and plans a calm, fair stand.

passage: Friday: at dinner, Farhan's mother said Rukhsar should stop working late now that she was married. Rukhsar looked at Farhan. He looked at his plate. His brother Zubin changed the subject to cricket. That night Rukhsar slept facing the wall. Tuesday: his mother complained that Rukhsar never asked her opinion; Rukhsar complained that Farhan never defended her. Farhan felt like a rope pulled at both ends, and he stayed late at the office to avoid them both. The next Sunday: at lunch, Farhan put down his spoon. 'Ammi, Rukhsar's late shifts are our decision, and I'm proud of her work. Rukhsar, Ammi misses you in the evenings. Can we keep Sundays for family lunch?' His mother sniffed, but agreed. Rukhsar squeezed his hand under the table. Zubin grinned at his rice.

qa.q: What did Zubin do when Rukhsar looked at Farhan on Friday?
qa.a: He changed the subject to cricket.

qa.q: What was Farhan feeling on Tuesday?
qa.a: He felt torn and trapped, like a rope pulled at both ends, so he stayed late at the office to avoid them both.

qa.q: What made Farhan's Sunday stand work?
qa.a: He stated the decision calmly and fairly, backing Rukhsar's work while naming his mother's feelings and offering Sunday lunches.

qa.q: How did Farhan's silence on Friday affect Rukhsar?
qa.a: She felt unsupported and hurt, and slept facing the wall that night.

grounding: Over a week a young husband moves from silent avoidance between his mother and wife to a calm, fair stand that respects both.

passage: Suraj, you think your wife and your parents will sort it out if you keep quiet? Listen to your Binita pishi. When I married your pishemoshai, my father wanted him to join our family tea business in Guwahati. He wanted to stay with his railway job. Every visit, Baba lectured, your pishemoshai went stiff, and I just served more fish. I thought silence kept the peace. It didn't. Baba thought I didn't respect him, and my husband thought I secretly agreed with Baba. Both of them felt alone, and so did I. One Bijoya evening I finally said, 'Baba, he is staying with the railways, and I support him. But we'll come every holiday and help at the garden.' Baba didn't speak to me for a week. After that, things were better than they had been in a year.

qa.q: What job did Binita's husband want to keep?
qa.a: His railway job.

qa.q: Why did young Binita keep serving more fish during the lectures?
qa.a: She was anxious and torn, hoping silence would keep the peace between her father and her husband.

qa.q: Which choice in the story changed things, and why?
qa.a: Speaking up on Bijoya evening with a calm, fair stand, backing her husband's job while offering holiday visits and help, so both men knew where she stood.

qa.q: How did Baba feel during those silent years?
qa.a: He felt disrespected and alone, thinking his daughter did not value his wishes.

grounding: An aunt recalls how staying silent between her father and husband left everyone unsupported until she took a calm, fair stand.

passage: The movers wanted to leave by four, the rain was coming in sideways, and Manoj's mother stood in the doorway of the new flat with the key to Dadi's huge carved almirah. 'This goes in the bedroom. It's family.' Kritika, soaked, shook her head. 'There's no space, Mummy. We agreed it goes to storage.' Both of them turned to Manoj. His younger brother Ujjwal, carrying boxes, froze on the stairs. Manoj's first thought was to mumble and let the movers decide. Instead he took a breath. 'Mummy, Kritika's right that it won't fit, and I agreed to storage. But I know it matters to you. Let's store it for now and find it a place when we get a bigger flat.' His mother's lips tightened. Kritika touched his arm. The movers carried the almirah back to the truck.

qa.q: By what time did the movers want to leave?
qa.a: By four.

qa.q: What was Manoj tempted to do when both women turned to him, and why?
qa.a: He felt torn and pressured, and his first impulse was to mumble and let the movers decide, avoiding taking a side.

qa.q: What made Manoj's answer a fair stand?
qa.a: He agreed with Kritika's facts and their earlier decision while naming why the almirah matters to his mother and offering a later plan.

qa.q: What is it like for Ujjwal, frozen on the stairs?
qa.a: He is caught watching a tense family moment, probably uneasy and unsure whether to step in, and relieved when Manoj settles it.

grounding: A young husband caught between his mother and wife on a rushed, rainy moving day chooses a calm, fair stand over silence.

passage: In the Kothrud flat, the argument had been circling since breakfast. Pradeep's mother wanted the puja for the new flat on Saturday, when the priest was free. Swati had already promised that Saturday to her parents, who were coming from Nagpur. Pradeep's father kept repeating, "The priest decides, not us." Pradeep scrolled his phone. For two days he had said nothing, and both women had noticed. Swati slept facing the wall. His mother told him he had "changed after marriage". On Thursday evening he put the phone face down on the dining table. "Aai, Swati's parents booked their tickets first. Swati, Aai has waited years for this puja. Can we ask the priest about Sunday morning? I'll call him myself." His mother sighed, then nodded slowly. Under the table, Swati squeezed his hand.

qa.q: Why could Swati not keep Saturday free?
qa.a: Swati had already promised that Saturday to her parents, who were coming from Nagpur.

qa.q: What was Pradeep feeling while he scrolled his phone for two days?
qa.a: He felt torn and uneasy between his mother and Swati, and hid behind the phone rather than risk upsetting either of them.

qa.q: What went wrong at first, and what fixed it?
qa.a: His silence left both his mother and Swati feeling unsupported; naming each side's fair point and offering to call the priest himself turned it into a shared plan.

qa.q: What was it like for Swati while Pradeep stayed quiet?
qa.a: She probably felt alone in the disagreement, which is why she slept facing the wall; squeezing his hand shows her relief when he finally spoke up fairly.

grounding: Shows a young husband torn between his parents and his wife, where silence hurts both and a calm, fair stand protects both relationships.
